paragraphs.heading: An ending with nothing left to do
paragraphs.text: The heat death of the universe, also called the Big Chill or the Big Freeze, is a hypothesis about how the universe ends. It says the universe will reach a state with no thermodynamic free energy left. Having hit maximum entropy, it could no longer run any thermodynamic process at all. Physicists call this state thermodynamic equilibrium. Heat death does not require any particular temperature; it only means that temperature differences and other processes can no longer be used to do work.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea comes from
paragraphs.text: The idea grows out of the second law of thermodynamics, which in one version says entropy tends to increase in an isolated system. Applied to the universe, it suggests that if the universe lasts long enough, it will come ever closer to a state where all energy is spread evenly. In this view, nature tends to turn motion into heat. Carried far enough, the mechanical movement of the universe would slowly run down as work is turned into heat.

paragraphs.heading: Early thinkers
paragraphs.text: The thought that everything in the universe cools until it is too cold for life seems to have come first from the French astronomer Jean Sylvain Bailly in 1777. He held that every planet has inner heat and is at some stage of cooling. Venus, in his view, was still too hot for life, while Mars was already too cold. Tying heat death to the laws of thermodynamics came later, starting in 1851 with Lord Kelvin, who built on work by Sadi Carnot, James Joule and Rudolf Clausius. Hermann von Helmholtz and William Rankine developed his views over the next decade.

paragraphs.heading: Kelvin's paradox
paragraphs.text: Kelvin also raised what is now called the heat death paradox. It cast doubt on the classical belief that the universe is infinitely old, because equilibrium has not yet been reached, so more work and entropy production are still possible. The very existence of stars and temperature differences can be taken as evidence that the universe is not infinitely old. Even so, Kelvin himself was unsure whether the universe would ever reach equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: The modern picture
paragraphs.text: If space is flat or hyperbolic in its curvature, or if dark energy takes the form of a positive cosmological constant, the universe should keep expanding forever, and a heat death is expected. In such an ever-expanding universe, a Big Rip is the other possible end. With a cosmological constant of zero, the temperature would sink toward absolute zero over a very long time. With a positive one, it would level off at a value above zero, while entropy reaches its maximum and no more work is possible.

paragraphs.heading: Doubts and loopholes
paragraphs.text: Some have suggested that, over immense spans of time, entropy could drop on its own through thermal fluctuations and related effects. A new Big Bang might then create a universe like ours through quantum fluctuations and tunnelling, in roughly 10^(10^10⁵⁶) years. Others question the premise itself. Max Planck held that speaking of the universe's entropy is meaningless, since it cannot be defined accurately. Lee Smolin argues that gravity matters for keeping the universe out of equilibrium: in systems bound by gravity, the parts speed up when energy is taken away, and such systems grow more structured instead of evening out.
